q: A phlebotomist is preparing a patient's antecubital site for a blood culture using chlorhexidine gluconate. How long should the scrub be performed before the site is allowed to dry?
choices: 10 seconds
15 seconds
30 seconds
2 minutes
why: Chlorhexidine gluconate requires a 30-second friction scrub followed by complete air drying to kill skin flora. A 15-second scrub is the common distractor but does not provide adequate contact time, and undried antiseptic can inhibit organism growth.

q: When blood cultures are collected with a syringe on an adult, which bottle is inoculated first and why?
choices: Aerobic, because air in the syringe would be pushed into the anaerobic bottle
Anaerobic, because anaerobes die fastest
Either bottle, because volume is what matters
Aerobic, because it holds more media
why: With a syringe draw, the aerobic bottle is filled first so residual air in the syringe hub does not enter the anaerobic bottle and kill the anaerobes. With a butterfly and holder the order reverses, which is why simply answering anaerobic first is wrong.

q: An adult blood culture set is being collected. What volume of blood should be placed in each bottle?
choices: 1 to 3 mL
3 to 5 mL
5 to 7 mL
8 to 10 mL
why: Adult bottles require 8 to 10 mL each because bacteremia is often low level and sensitivity rises with volume. The 1 to 3 mL range applies to pediatric bottles, not adults.

q: A provider orders two sets of blood cultures. Which collection approach is correct?
choices: Both sets from the same vein back to back
Two sets drawn from two separate venipuncture sites
One set from a vein and one from a capillary stick
Both sets from the existing peripheral IV
why: Two sets from two different sites let the lab distinguish true bacteremia from skin contamination, since the same organism in both sites suggests true infection. Drawing both from one site defeats that comparison.

q: A blood culture grows coagulase-negative Staphylococcus in one bottle of one set only, while the second site is negative. This pattern most likely indicates which of the following?
choices: Skin flora contamination during collection
True gram-negative sepsis
Endocarditis requiring immediate surgery
A false-negative culture
why: A common skin organism growing in only one bottle of one set is the classic picture of contamination from inadequate antisepsis. True bacteremia typically produces growth in both sets drawn from separate sites.

q: When is the optimal time to collect blood cultures relative to a patient's fever and antibiotic schedule?
choices: At the peak of the fever, after the antibiotic dose
Twenty-four hours after antibiotics are started
As the fever is rising and before the next antibiotic dose
Only when the patient is afebrile
why: Organism concentration is highest as the temperature spikes, and drawing before the antibiotic dose (at the trough) avoids drug suppression of growth. Collecting after the dose lowers recovery of the organism.

q: A patient needs blood cultures, a light blue citrate tube, a green heparin tube, and a lavender EDTA tube. Which is collected first?
choices: Light blue citrate
Blood culture bottles
Green heparin
Lavender EDTA
why: Sterile blood culture bottles always precede all other tubes in the CLSI order of draw to protect sterility. Light blue is first among the additive tubes but still follows the cultures.

q: A phlebotomist is collecting a newborn screening card by heelstick. Which technique is correct?
choices: Layer several small drops into each circle until filled
Press the card directly against the heel and smear
Fill the circles from both sides of the paper
Apply one large free-flowing drop to fill each circle completely
why: Each circle must be filled with a single large drop allowed to soak through and saturate the paper evenly. Layering multiple drops creates uneven saturation and is a top cause of rejected newborn screening cards.

q: After collection, how should a newborn screening card be handled before transport?
choices: Sealed in a plastic bag immediately
Placed under a warming lamp to speed drying
Air dried flat at room temperature away from heat and sunlight
Refrigerated while still wet
why: The card must dry flat in open air at room temperature for at least three hours; heat, sunlight, and sealing in plastic denature the analytes. A warming lamp accelerates drying but destroys specimen integrity.

q: A bilirubin specimen is collected on a jaundiced neonate. What special handling is required?
choices: Protect the specimen from light using an amber tube or foil wrap
Keep the specimen at 37 degrees C
Place the specimen in an ice slurry
Agitate the specimen continuously
why: Bilirubin is photosensitive and can degrade significantly within an hour of light exposure, falsely lowering results. Chilling is required for ammonia and lactic acid, not bilirubin.

q: A cold agglutinin specimen is ordered. Which handling is correct?
choices: Chill in ice water immediately after collection
Collect in EDTA and refrigerate
Warm the tube to 37 degrees C and keep it warm until the serum is separated
Freeze the specimen within 30 minutes
why: Cold agglutinins attach to red cells below body temperature, so the specimen must be prewarmed and maintained at 37 degrees C until serum separation. Refrigerating it removes the antibody from the serum and falsely lowers the titer.

q: Which of the following specimens requires transport in an ice slurry?
choices: Cold agglutinins
Ammonia and lactic acid
Bilirubin
Cryoglobulins
why: Ammonia and lactic acid rise rapidly through in vitro cell metabolism, so chilling slows that change. Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins require 37 degrees C transport, the opposite condition.

q: A three-hour glucose tolerance test is ordered. Which patient preparation is correct?
choices: The patient may eat a light breakfast before the fasting draw
The patient should chew gum to stay hydrated
The patient should smoke to reduce anxiety
The patient fasts 8 to 12 hours, and may drink only water before the fasting specimen
why: A valid GTT begins with a true 8 to 12 hour fast in which only water is permitted. Gum, food, and smoking all stimulate digestion or glucose changes and invalidate the baseline.

q: During a glucose tolerance test, the timing of each timed specimen is counted from which point?
choices: The time the patient finishes drinking the glucose beverage
The time the fasting specimen was drawn
The time the patient arrived at the lab
The time the provider ordered the test
why: All timed intervals start the moment the patient finishes the glucose load, since that is when absorption begins. Timing from the fasting draw shifts every subsequent collection and makes the curve uninterpretable.

q: Thirty minutes into a glucose tolerance test, a patient vomits the glucose beverage. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Continue the test and note the vomiting later
Give a second glucose drink and restart the clock
Notify the provider, who decides whether to stop or reschedule the test
Collect all remaining specimens early
why: Vomiting means the glucose load was not absorbed, so the provider must decide whether to abort or reschedule. A phlebotomist may not independently redose a patient with glucose.

q: A trough level for vancomycin should be collected at which time?
choices: Immediately before the next scheduled dose
Thirty minutes after the infusion ends
Halfway between two doses
Any time during the infusion
why: The trough is the lowest concentration and is drawn immediately before the next dose, usually within 30 minutes of it. A specimen drawn 30 minutes after the infusion reflects the peak, not the trough.

q: A gentamicin peak level is ordered. When is it typically collected?
choices: Immediately before the dose
Twelve hours after the dose
Twenty-four hours after the dose
About 30 minutes after the IV infusion is complete
why: Peak levels for aminoglycosides are drawn about 30 minutes after the end of an IV infusion, when distribution is complete. Drawing before the dose yields the trough and would be reported incorrectly if labeled a peak.

q: A digoxin level is ordered on a patient who received an oral dose one hour ago. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Draw immediately since digoxin is stable
Draw and mark the specimen as a peak
Notify the nurse that digoxin levels require at least 8 hours after the dose for equilibration
Refuse the order outright
why: Digoxin distributes slowly into tissue, so a level drawn before roughly 8 hours post-dose is falsely elevated. Drawing it early and labeling it a peak would mislead the provider into reducing a correct dose.

q: Which site preparation is required for a legal blood alcohol collection?
choices: 70 percent isopropyl alcohol
A non-alcohol antiseptic such as povidone-iodine or benzalkonium chloride
Chlorhexidine gluconate with alcohol base
No antiseptic at all
why: An alcohol-based prep can contaminate the specimen and is indefensible in court, so a non-alcohol antiseptic is used. Isopropyl alcohol is the standard venipuncture prep but is specifically prohibited here.

q: Which tube is generally used for a blood alcohol specimen, and why?
choices: Lavender EDTA, to prevent clotting
Light blue citrate, to preserve plasma
Red serum tube, because no additive interferes
Gray sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, because fluoride inhibits glycolysis and microbial alcohol production
why: Sodium fluoride in the gray tube blocks glycolysis and stops microbes from fermenting glucose into ethanol, which would falsely raise the result. A red serum tube offers no such preservative protection.

q: A blood alcohol specimen is collected for law enforcement. What documentation is required?
choices: A standard requisition only
A chain of custody form documenting every person who handles the specimen
A verbal report to the officer
A copy of the patient's chart
why: Forensic specimens require an unbroken, signed chain of custody from collection through analysis to be admissible. A routine requisition does not document transfer of possession.

q: During a urine drug screen collection, the specimen temperature must be checked within what time frame?
choices: Within 4 minutes of voiding
Within 15 minutes
Within 30 minutes
Within 1 hour
why: The temperature strip must be read within 4 minutes, and an acceptable range is 32.5 to 37.7 degrees C, to detect a substituted specimen. Waiting 15 or 30 minutes lets the sample cool and destroys the check.

q: In a federally regulated split specimen drug collection, how is the urine handled?
choices: The entire volume is sent as one sample
Two separate voids are collected an hour apart
The single void is divided into an A bottle for testing and a B bottle held for possible retest
The donor keeps half the sample
why: One void is split into bottles A and B, with B sealed and stored so the donor may request confirmatory retesting. Collecting two separate voids would not be a split of the same specimen and is not acceptable.

q: Which action best protects the integrity of a forensic specimen collection?
choices: Leaving the specimen at the nurses station for pickup
Sealing the specimen in tamper-evident packaging and documenting each transfer with signatures and times
Labeling the specimen after transport
Storing it unlabeled in a locked drawer
why: Tamper-evident sealing plus signed, timed transfers proves the specimen was never altered or exchanged. Any unattended or unlabeled interval breaks the chain and makes the result inadmissible.

q: A phlebotomist is collecting specimens for paternity testing. Which requirement applies?
choices: Positive identification of every participant with photo ID, chain of custody, and specimens from mother, child, and alleged father
Only the child needs to be identified
Specimens may be collected at home and mailed in
Verbal identification by a relative is sufficient
why: Parentage testing is a legal collection requiring photo identification of each party and full chain of custody on all three specimens. Relying on a relative to vouch for identity would invalidate the result in court.

q: Before drawing a type and crossmatch, which identification step is required?
choices: Confirm the room number with the unit clerk
Ask the patient to confirm the ordering provider
Check the chart for a prior blood type
Compare the patient's stated name and date of birth to the ID band and requisition, and apply the blood bank identification band
why: Active identification against the ID band plus a blood bank band that links the patient to the specimen prevents fatal ABO mismatches. Room number is never an acceptable identifier because patients are moved.

q: A blood bank specimen label must include which item not required on a routine chemistry label?
choices: Test name
Patient name
Date of collection
The phlebotomist's initials and the blood bank band number tying the specimen to the patient
why: The blood bank band number and collector identification create a traceable link from the crossmatch specimen to the patient at the bedside. Name and date appear on routine labels too and do not provide that link.

q: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery donates units of her own blood in advance. This is called what?
choices: Directed donation
Therapeutic phlebotomy
Autologous donation
Apheresis
why: Autologous donation means the patient donates blood for her own later transfusion, eliminating compatibility and disease transmission risk. A directed donation comes from a specific person chosen by the patient, not from the patient herself.

q: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis has a standing order for unit removal. This procedure is best described as which of the following?
choices: Therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce iron overload
Autologous donation for future use
Plasmapheresis
A diagnostic venipuncture
why: Therapeutic phlebotomy removes a unit of blood as treatment, lowering iron stores in hemochromatosis or red cell mass in polycythemia vera. The blood is removed for treatment, not banked for the patient's own transfusion as in autologous donation.

q: What is the approximate volume of a standard whole blood donor unit?
choices: 250 mL
350 mL
450 to 500 mL
750 mL
why: A standard whole blood unit is about 450 to 500 mL, roughly one pint, collected into anticoagulant. Drawing 750 mL would exceed the safe limit for a single donation.

q: A 19-year-old weighing 108 pounds with a hemoglobin of 13.5 g/dL wishes to donate whole blood. What is the correct action?
choices: Accept the donor, since the hemoglobin is adequate
Defer the donor, because the minimum weight for whole blood donation is 110 pounds
Defer the donor because of age
Accept but collect only half a unit
why: Allogeneic whole blood donors must weigh at least 110 pounds so that the approximately 500 mL draw is a safe fraction of blood volume. The hemoglobin and age both meet criteria, which makes weight the only disqualifier.

q: Before radial artery puncture, the modified Allen test is performed to determine what?
choices: That collateral circulation from the ulnar artery is adequate
That the patient is not anemic
That the radial pulse is strong
That the patient is not on anticoagulants
why: The modified Allen test confirms the ulnar artery can perfuse the hand if the radial artery becomes occluded after puncture. A strong radial pulse says nothing about collateral ulnar flow, which is the actual safety concern.

q: A modified Allen test is performed and the hand does not flush within 15 seconds after the ulnar artery is released. What does this mean?
choices: The test is positive and the site may be used
The patient is dehydrated
The phlebotomist should puncture the brachial artery instead without further evaluation
The test is negative and that radial artery must not be used
why: Failure to flush indicates inadequate ulnar collateral circulation, so puncturing that radial artery risks ischemia of the hand. Selecting another site is a provider decision, not an automatic move to the brachial artery by the phlebotomist.

q: Which syringe and handling combination is correct for an arterial blood gas specimen?
choices: A plain syringe transported at room temperature
A heparinized syringe with air bubbles expelled, capped and transported per protocol, often in ice slurry if delayed
An EDTA syringe kept at 37 degrees C
A citrate syringe protected from light
why: ABGs require heparin anticoagulation, immediate removal of air bubbles because room air alters pO2 and pCO2, and chilling when analysis is delayed beyond 30 minutes. EDTA is never used because it alters pH.

q: Who may perform an arterial puncture for blood gases?
choices: Any phlebotomist after basic venipuncture training
Only personnel with documented specialized arterial puncture training, such as respiratory therapists, nurses, or specially trained phlebotomists
A patient care technician under general supervision
Any staff member certified in CPR
why: Arterial puncture carries risk of hemorrhage, nerve injury, and thrombosis, so it requires documented advanced training and institutional authorization. Routine venipuncture certification alone does not qualify a phlebotomist.

q: A capillary blood gas is ordered on an infant. Which step is essential to a valid result?
choices: Squeezing the heel firmly to obtain flow quickly
Using the central plantar surface of the heel
Air drying the sample before capping
Prewarming the site and collecting free-flowing blood without air bubbles in the capillary tube
why: Prewarming arterializes capillary blood and free flow without bubbles preserves gas values; squeezing introduces tissue fluid and falsely alters results. The central plantar surface risks bone injury and is never used for heelsticks.

q: A glucose meter quality control result falls outside the acceptable range. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Run the patient sample anyway and flag the result
Repeat the control once and report the patient result regardless
Adjust the meter reading manually
Remove the meter from use, document the failure, and troubleshoot or use a backup device before testing patients
why: An out of range control means patient results from that device cannot be trusted, so it must be taken out of service until resolved. Reporting a flagged patient result on a failed device still releases unreliable data.

q: A point-of-care glucose reads critically high on a symptomatic patient. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Notify the provider and collect a venous specimen for laboratory confirmation
Repeat the POC test three more times and average the values
Document the result and take no further action
Discard the result as an obvious error
why: Critical POC values are screening results and must be confirmed by a laboratory method while the provider is notified promptly. Averaging repeated POC readings does not improve accuracy and delays treatment.

q: A patient must collect a 24-hour urine specimen. Which instruction is correct?
choices: Save every void including the first morning specimen that starts the collection
Refrigerate only the final sample
Discard the first void, then collect all urine for 24 hours including the void at the end of the period, keeping the container cool
Collect only daytime voids
why: The timed period starts with an empty bladder, so the first void is discarded and the final void at the 24-hour mark is included, with refrigeration or a preservative maintained throughout. Saving that first void adds urine made before the timed period and falsely raises analyte totals.

q: A phlebotomist is instructing a female patient on a clean-catch midstream urine collection. Which instruction is correct?
choices: Collect the very first portion of the stream
Cleanse from front to back, begin voiding into the toilet, then collect the midstream portion in the sterile cup
Cleanse after voiding to avoid contaminating the wipe
Use tap water only, since antiseptic wipes interfere with culture
why: Front to back cleansing plus discarding the initial stream washes away urethral and perineal flora so the midstream portion reflects bladder urine. Collecting the first portion carries the highest contamination and commonly causes mixed-flora culture rejection.
